characterList.description: President-elect of Haiti. He has dark skin, is bald, and wears a dark suit with a blue tie and a small Haitian flag pin on his lapel.
characterList.name: Michel Martelly

characterList.description: Director of the CSIS Americas Program. He has light skin, short grey hair, a grey mustache, and wears glasses, a dark suit with a red patterned tie.
characterList.name: Stephen Johnson

content_metadata.description: A video analysis focusing on an interview with Michel Martelly and Stephen Johnson, discussing the future of Haiti.

narrativeProgression.description: Stephen Johnson poses a question about Martelly's top priorities upon taking office.

Martelly outlines his priorities, including addressing the cholera outbreak, relocating people from tent cities, combating the rising cost of living, focusing on education and agricultural reform, and restoring trust in the government.
Stephen Johnson thanks Martelly for the interview.
Martelly expresses his gratitude and anticipates CSIS expertise to assist in Haiti's success.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: President-elect Marteli, welcome to CSIS.
Coming into office, you have very little time to confront some very serious challenges
and also some opportunities that are coming your way with donors and also new initiatives
that people in Haiti are ready for.
What do you consider your top three priorities coming into office?
First of all, thank you, Steve, for having me and I want to thank the members of CSIS.
And I will tell you that we've been caught by surprise.
At first we had identified the cholera issue as a priority, as an urgency.
We had identified the relocation of the people under the tent as a priority.
And things are changing.
Now the price of the fuel is going up, so we have to get ready for crisis on Chris Alimatera,
a food crisis, as the price of the products are going high on the international market.
Price of oil is going up and it's like things are changing on us.
So we are planning on, we are actually talking to our importators.
We are working on cutting the tax that we perceive on these products.
And the cholera remains an issue because if we don't focus on it then it will spread again.
And as another issue we have, the people living under those tents,
it's been over 14 months and they are still living under the tents.
And not much is being done.
And I believe if a little bit was done, we would have seen progress
because some of these tents are fake tents.
People are using these tents to make business.
They come when there is food distribution.
They come when they are about to promise Alim to a tent owner
and whenever the organization is in charge of that it leaves, they leave too.
But way before the earthquake, lodging housing was an issue
and it's going to be one of our priority.
Education is another priority for us.
As we have identified ignorance as a vector who produce,
who generates poverty.
So it will be very important for us to finally bring our kids to school.
The constitution made predicts, mandates, free schooling.
But unfortunately our past leaders have never tried to implement.
So I think it's a risk responsibility that I have
as I understand the need for every child to go to school.
And the last one will be the agriculture we form that we need to do.
We will be creating wealth, we will be bringing food security.
We will be stepping that migration towards the big cities.
We will be opening a window on decreasing importation.
So these are the aspects that have been the theme that have been campaigning on.
But we must remember that everything else remains a priority in Haiti.
Starting from clean water, security, a land title.
And so on the state of law, transparency, eradicating corruption.
These are issues that we must address as we need,
we understand the need to rebuild that confidence to build a confidence back
between the people of Haiti and the government itself.
And confidence between Haiti and its partners is very important to do that.
Even rebuilding that confidence should be a priority.
Well, that's a lot of responsibility to rest on your shoulders
as well as the shoulders of the members of your administration.
But at the same time, you have quite a bit of talent in the Haitian people.
What strengths do you think the people of Haiti bring to this task of moving forward?
Well, I think this is the greatest opportunity that we have
because the people of Haiti are directly implicated this time.
They have voted in mass because they wanted a rupture
with a state or a traditional politics that have shown no results.
And because of that, they now they feel like they have fought that fight.
They have won.
They have an overtroist system who has a failed system.
And now they are already taking to the streets and cleaning the streets.
They're waiting for orders.
You know, they want to implicate themselves.
They're willing to suffer.
They're willing to move out of tents.
They're willing to move out of neighborhoods.
They understand that most of the decisions we will have to take
are not going to be popular measures.
And they're willing to suffer because they identify in this new leader
that I am a light at the end of the turner.
And because of that, I believe it's...
They're going to play a very important role.
And I have a campaigning tell in them that I was going to count on them
as much as they do count on me.
And together and with our partners with the international community
behind one dream, all this weight that you have identified on my shoulder.
It will remain a weight, but it will be easier for us to succeed.
Mr. President-elect, thank you so much for visiting us this afternoon at CSIS.
Thank you so much and no need to tell you that I'll be expecting CSIS expertise
also for us to succeed.
Thank you.
My pleasure.
